question: What led you to choose that one over the others?
response:
Honestly, it took me a minute. A few of them spoke to me - I almost grabbed the planet one because climate is such a huge part of my work, and the women's leadership one is something I deeply believe in.

But I kept coming back to this one. Immigration and border policy has been weighing on me so much lately. The bilingual element really got me - it's not just a statement, it's embodying the idea right there in the object itself. English and Spanish together on the same ribbon. That feels meaningful.

And I think because I'm from out of state, visiting here near DC, there's something about being in this area where these policies actually get made that made it feel more urgent. Like I wanted to carry something out of here that reflects what I think is one of the most pressing human rights issues right now.

Also, if I'm being honest, the ribbon is going to end up somewhere people can see it - maybe on my bag or in my office - and I think this one will prompt conversations in a way that feels important to me. It might make someone think, or ask me about it, and that matters.

The others felt more like things I'd nod along to. This one felt like something I needed to actually hold.

question: What led you to choose that one over the others?
response:
Honestly, it spoke to me most directly given the work I do. In the nonprofit world, especially in program work, you're constantly thinking about who gets resources, who gets access, who gets left out of systems. The bilingual text felt important too - it's not just saying the words in English, it's embodying the idea by including Spanish right there alongside it. That felt more honest somehow, more like it was actually doing the thing it was saying rather than just declaring it.

The immigration piece is real for me too. It's something I care about politically and something that intersects with communities we fund. So it felt personal, not just abstract.

The others are good, I mean I agree with all of them honestly, that's a little awkward actually, standing there choosing between things you believe in. The Ruth Bader Ginsburg quote about women belonging in all places, I almost took that one. And planet before profits, that's not wrong either.

But there was something about the border one that felt more urgent to me right now, given what's happening politically. And I liked that it would travel home with me, out of state, across whatever invisible lines we draw. That felt right for what it's saying.

I'll be honest, I'm also just a little moved that an art museum is doing this, letting you take something. I wasn't expecting that.

question: What led you to choose that one over the others?
response:
Honestly, a few things converged. The bilingual text was the first thing that caught my attention visually - it signals something about who the message is for, and who it's addressing. Living in DC, immigration policy is constantly in the air, and I work adjacent to some of that world as a contractor, so it feels immediate and not abstract to me.

I also think it's the one that challenges something most fundamentally - not just a policy position but an entire framework for how we organize the world and who gets to move through it freely. The others felt more like affirmations of things that are either already broadly accepted in the circles I move in, or more narrowly focused.

I'll be honest that I hesitated over the Ruth Bader Ginsburg quote about women belonging in all places where decisions are made. That one has real weight. But it's also been so thoroughly absorbed into a kind of mainstream liberal iconography at this point - you see it everywhere - that wearing it feels less like a statement and more like a signal of belonging to a particular demographic. I'm a little wary of that.

The borders one still has some friction to it. Not everyone who considers themselves progressive is fully on board with what it actually implies if you take it seriously. That tension is interesting to me. I'd rather wear something that starts a conversation than something that just gets nodded at.

question: What led you to choose that one over the others?
response:
Honestly, a few things pulled me toward it.

The bilingual text feels important to me, especially being in DC where immigration policy is so present and contested. It feels more specific and grounded than some of the others, which read a bit more like general sentiment.

I also work as a federal contractor, so I'm actually pretty conscious about what I put on display publicly. Some of the others gave me pause for that reason. FREE SPEECH MAKES FREE PEOPLE felt ambiguous to me - that framing gets used in ways I'm not always comfortable with. PLANET BEFORE PROFITS I agree with but it felt almost too broad. NOT HERE TO BE LIKED felt more like a personal statement than a political one.

WOMEN BELONG IN ALL PLACES WHERE DECISIONS ARE MADE is a message I genuinely support, but wearing it felt a little bit like it wasn't mine to wear, if that makes sense - I wanted to be thoughtful about that.

WITHOUT BORDERS felt like the one where I was most willing to be seen and to stand behind it clearly, even in a space like this where I don't know who else is visiting. There's also something I appreciate about the artwork making you do that calculus - think about what you're willing to wear publicly, what you're willing to claim. That tension is part of what the piece is doing, I think.
